title: The limping child: irritable hip at age 6

header.contentArea: Paediatric orthopaedics: the irritable hip (findings and results released in stages)
guidelineVersions: BOAST: The management of children with acute musculoskeletal infection (May 2022)
UK consensus on paediatric musculoskeletal infection (Bone Joint J, July 2023)
Kocher et al., J Bone Joint Surg Am (1999 and 2004)

related.why: Septic arthritis of the native knee in adults

brief.role: Core surgical trainee in trauma and orthopaedics
brief.scenario: Oliver Petrie, 6, is brought by his mother with 3 days of right hip pain and a limp. There was no injury. He had a cold last week.
brief.task: The examiner will give you examination findings and results in stages. Discuss your differential diagnosis, interpretation and management.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Most irritable hips at this age are transient synovitis, but septic arthritis must be excluded first.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Treating a zero Kocher score as a rule-out, or thinking SUFE at age 6.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "I'd look for fever, weight-bearing and red flags, and examine hip, knee and spine."

grid.label: Assess and look for red flags
grid.fail: Diagnoses from the doorway without examining him.
grid.pass: Asks about fever, injury, recent illness, night pain and systemic upset; checks temperature, weight-bearing, hip, knee, spine and abdomen.
grid.high: Examines the knee because hip pain refers there, and considers safeguarding if the story does not fit.

grid.label: Differential by age
grid.fail: Anchors on SUFE, or omits septic arthritis.
grid.pass: Transient synovitis, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, Perthes disease, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, injury including non-accidental, and malignancy.
grid.high: At 6, transient synovitis and Perthes are likely; SUFE is an adolescent condition; septic arthritis is the one not to miss.

grid.label: Investigations
grid.fail: Requests only an X-ray, or no blood tests.
grid.pass: FBC, CRP, ESR and blood cultures; AP pelvis and frog-lateral X-rays; hip ultrasound for effusion.
grid.high: Knows ultrasound shows an effusion but not whether it is infected; MRI if doubt persists.

grid.label: Interpret results with the Kocher criteria
grid.fail: Says a low score excludes septic arthritis.
grid.pass: Kocher predictors: history of fever, non-weight-bearing, ESR 40 or more, white count over 12; none present, so septic arthritis is unlikely.
grid.high: Treats the score as support, not a rule-out: it performed less well on validation, and early CRP can be normal.

grid.label: Manage transient synovitis safely
grid.fail: Discharges with no plan or review.
grid.pass: Diagnosis of exclusion: analgesia with ibuprofen, rest, and a planned review.
grid.high: Gives explicit return criteria and arranges repeat X-rays if the limp persists, as early Perthes can be missed.

grid.label: Septic arthritis pathway (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Starts oral antibiotics and sends him home, or waits for the morning.
grid.pass: If suspected: urgent orthopaedic and paediatric referral, blood cultures, and aspiration or washout ideally within 24 hours of diagnosis.
grid.high: IV antibiotics immediately if septic; if stable with surgery imminent, deep samples first to guide treatment.

grid.label: Explain and safety-net
grid.fail: Tells the mother it is nothing and gives no advice.
grid.pass: Explains the likely diagnosis, the uncertainty and what would change it, with written safety-net advice.
grid.high: Addresses her worry directly, checks she can return quickly, and documents the advice.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: A 6-year-old with a limp. What are you thinking?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Probably a slipped upper femoral epiphysis.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: He's walking in, so I don't think he needs much examining. I'd get a hip X-ray.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: He has no fever history, he's weight-bearing, ESR 14 and white count 9.2.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: So his Kocher score is zero and septic arthritis is excluded.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What would you tell his mother?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It's nothing serious. He can go home, no need to come back.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: A 6-year-old with a limp. How would you assess him?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd ask about fever, injury, recent illness, night pain and whether he's unwell. Then temperature, whether he'll weight-bear, and examine the hip, knee, spine and abdomen.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Transient synovitis, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, Perthes disease, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, injury including non-accidental, and malignancy.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: FBC, CRP, ESR and blood cultures, AP pelvis and frog-lateral X-rays, and a hip ultrasound.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: No fever history, weight-bearing, ESR 14, white count 9.2, CRP 8. Small effusion on ultrasound. X-rays normal.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: None of the four Kocher predictors are present: fever history, non-weight-bearing, ESR 40 or more, white count over 12. Septic arthritis is unlikely.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Transient synovitis is a diagnosis of exclusion: ibuprofen, rest, and a planned review.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What if you suspected septic arthritis?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Urgent orthopaedic and paediatric referral, blood cultures, and aspiration or washout ideally within 24 hours.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What do you tell his mother?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: That this is most likely a temporary inflammation after his cold, what we're not yet sure of, and written advice on when to bring him back.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd examine the knee as well, because hip pain often refers there. If the story didn't fit his injuries, I'd think about safeguarding.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Unlikely at 6: SUFE is an adolescent condition. At his age, transient synovitis and Perthes are more likely, and septic arthritis is the one I mustn't miss.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The ultrasound shows an effusion. Does that mean infection?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: No, ultrasound can't tell a sterile effusion from pus. If I remained worried, MRI would help.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: So a Kocher score of zero rules out infection?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: It makes it unlikely, but it's support for judgement, not a rule-out. It performed less well when validated elsewhere, and CRP can be normal early. If he became febrile or stopped weight-bearing, I'd reassess.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Yes, with clear return criteria: fever, refusing to walk, worsening pain or a limp that doesn't settle. If it persists, repeat X-rays, as early Perthes can look normal.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: He returns febrile, refusing to weight-bear.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: If he meets sepsis criteria, IV antibiotics immediately after cultures. If he's stable and theatre is imminent, aspiration first so we get samples to guide treatment.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd ask what worries her most, check she can get back quickly, and document the advice I've given.

failures.move: Oral antibiotics and discharge for a febrile child who won't weight-bear.
failures.consequence: Septic arthritis destroys the joint; delayed drainage risks growth disturbance and sepsis.

failures.move: Using a zero Kocher score to stop thinking about infection.
failures.consequence: Early septic arthritis with normal markers is sent home.
Transient synovitis, Perthes and infection are under-investigated.

recovery.line: To be precise, it makes infection unlikely; I'd still safety-net and reassess if he becomes febrile or stops weight-bearing.

knowledge.fact: Kocher predictors: history of fever, non-weight-bearing, ESR 40 mm/h or more, WCC over 12 x 10^9/L. Probability under 0.2% with none, 93% with three.
The rule performed less well in a new population.
No algorithm is completely reliable; a normal CRP or ESR does not exclude early infection.
Septic arthritis: drainage ideally within 24 hours of diagnosis; IV antibiotics immediately if septic.
SUFE presents in adolescence; Perthes and transient synovitis in younger children.

recall.say: "Septic arthritis must be excluded before transient synovitis is diagnosed."
do: FBC, CRP, ESR, cultures; X-rays; ultrasound
Discharge only with safety-net and review
recall.trap: Kocher zero means infection is excluded.
recall.finish: Transient synovitis: analgesia and review. Septic: washout and IV antibiotics.

sources.name: Kocher MS, Zurakowski D, Kasser JR. Differentiating between septic arthritis and transient synovitis of the hip in children: an evidence-based clinical prediction algorithm. J Bone Joint Surg Am 1999;81:1662-70
sources.supports: Four independent predictors: history of fever, non-weight-bearing, ESR at least 40 mm/h, serum white cell count over 12 x 10^9/L; predicted probability of septic arthritis under 0.2% with none, 3.0% with one, 40.0% with two, 93.1% with three, 99.6% with four

sources.name: Kocher MS, Mandiga R, Zurakowski D, et al. Validation of a clinical prediction rule for the differentiation between septic arthritis and transient synovitis of the hip in children. J Bone Joint Surg Am 2004;86:1629-35
sources.supports: The same four predictors in a new population; diagnostic performance diminished on validation (area under the ROC curve 0.86 vs 0.96)

sources.name: British Orthopaedic Association Standard for Trauma and Orthopaedics (BOAST) with BSCOS: The management of children with acute musculoskeletal infection
sources.supports: Inpatient care under orthopaedic and paediatric specialists; FBC, CRP, blood cultures and ESR; MRI as preferred second-line imaging; empirical IV antibiotics immediately if high-risk sepsis criteria are met; if stable and surgery planned, antibiotics may be delayed for deep tissue sampling; septic arthritis needs surgical drainage as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours of diagnosis

sources.name: Mitchell PD, et al. Consensus guidelines on the management of musculoskeletal infection affecting children in the UK. Bone Joint J 2023;105-B:815-20
sources.supports: No single clinical algorithm is completely reliable; a normal CRP or ESR does not exclude infection early in the disease course; plain radiographs in all suspected cases; MRI as the preferred advanced imaging

sources.name: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery (O'Connell, McCaskie, Sayers, eds)
sources.supports: Paediatric hip disorders: transient synovitis, Perthes disease and slipped upper femoral epiphysis, and their typical ages

partner.opening: Oliver, 6, has had right hip pain and a limp for 3 days. No injury. He had a cold last week. How would you assess him?
partner.actorBrief: You are the examiner. Release findings and results only when the candidate asks. If the candidate uses Kocher as a rule-out, push on it.

reveals.trigger: Asks for history and observations, or examines (stage 1)
reveals.finding: No history of fever. T 37.4°C, HR 100. Walks with an antalgic limp but bears weight. Right hip: pain at the end of internal rotation. Knee, spine and abdomen normal. No bruising. Story consistent.
WCC 9.2 x 10^9/L, CRP 8 mg/L, ESR 14 mm/h. Blood cultures sent.
AP pelvis and frog-lateral X-rays normal. Ultrasound: small right hip effusion.

push.question: What is your differential?
push.expect: Transient synovitis, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, Perthes, JIA, injury including NAI, malignancy.

push.question: What investigations?
push.expect: FBC, CRP, ESR, blood cultures; AP and frog-lateral X-rays; ultrasound.

push.question: Apply the Kocher criteria.
push.expect: None of four present; septic arthritis unlikely but not excluded.

push.question: How will you manage him?
push.expect: Analgesia, rest, safety-net, planned review; repeat X-rays if limp persists.

push.question: What if septic arthritis were suspected?
push.expect: Urgent orthopaedic and paediatric care; cultures; drainage within 24 hours; IV antibiotics.

curveballs.prompt: He comes back 24 hours later: T 38.9°C and refusing to stand.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Now two or more predictors: treat as septic arthritis; urgent orthopaedic referral, cultures, aspiration or washout, IV antibiotics.

curveballs.prompt: Instead he is a 13-year-old with knee pain and an externally rotated leg.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Suspect SUFE: stop weight-bearing, AP and lateral X-rays of both hips, urgent orthopaedic fixation.

curveballs.prompt: His mother mentions night sweats, pallor and bruising.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Consider leukaemia: blood film and urgent paediatric review.

curveballs.prompt: Six weeks later he still limps.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Repeat hip X-rays for Perthes and orthopaedic follow-up.
